title: THE LAW THAT FORBADE A MAN FROM SLEEPING WITH HIS BROTHER’S WIFE—AND THE EXCEPTION THAT CHANGES EVERYTHING
paragraphs: THE LAW THAT FORBADE A MAN FROM SLEEPING WITH HIS BROTHER’S WIFE—AND THE EXCEPTION THAT CHANGES EVERYTHING

One verse called it a forbidden relationship. Another commanded a brother to marry the widow. Was God contradicting Himself—or was He revealing something extraordinary about holiness, mercy, family redemption, and the bloodline that would eventually lead to Jesus Christ?
There is a moment in Scripture when two commandments appear to collide.
And if you read them too quickly, you might walk away believing the Bible contradicts itself.
But stay with me.

Because buried inside these ancient laws is a story about a woman facing an uncertain future, a family name on the verge of disappearing, a man who refused his responsibility, and a God who cared about people the world could easily forget.
And eventually, this story will take us somewhere unexpected.
To a widow named Ruth.
To a family in Bethlehem.
And ultimately, to Jesus Christ.
But first, we need to confront the question that makes this passage so uncomfortable.
How could God forbid a man from taking his brother’s wife in one passage, then require a brother to marry his deceased brother’s widow in another?
The answer is not found by ignoring either commandment.
It is found by understanding why God gave both.
In Leviticus 18:16, Scripture declares:
“Thou shalt not uncover the nakedness of thy brother's wife: it is thy brother's nakedness.” — Leviticus 18:16, KJV
Those words are direct.
The expression “uncover the nakedness” is not merely about seeing someone without clothing. In the legal context of Leviticus 18, it is a Hebrew expression referring to prohibited sexual relations.
The original Hebrew reads:
עֶרְוַת אֵשֶׁת־אָחִיךָ לֹא תְגַלֵּה
ʿErvat eshet-ʾakhikha lo tegalleh.
Literally, the command means, “You shall not uncover the nakedness of your brother’s wife.”
The language is deliberately serious because marriage is not something God treats casually.
A brother’s wife was not someone another brother could simply claim because he desired her.
There were boundaries.
There was covenantal faithfulness.
There was a moral distinction between what someone wanted and what God permitted.
And that distinction still matters.
Because not every desire becomes righteous simply because the heart feels strongly about it.
Not every relationship becomes holy because two people call it love.
Sometimes the very boundary we resent is the boundary protecting someone else from betrayal.
But then we turn a few pages forward.
And suddenly, the law appears to say something astonishing.
Deuteronomy 25:5 declares:

“If brethren dwell together, and one of them die, and have no child, the wife of the dead shall not marry without unto a stranger: her husband's brother shall go in unto her, and take her to him to wife, and perform the duty of an husband's brother unto her.” — Deuteronomy 25:5, KJV
Read that again.
The brother is now instructed to marry the widow.
The very relationship that would ordinarily be forbidden becomes a specifically regulated duty under particular circumstances.
Was God changing His mind?
No.
The circumstances changed. And the purpose of the commandment was different.
Leviticus 18:16 established the ordinary prohibition against sexual relations with a brother’s wife.
Leviticus 20:21 reinforced that prohibition.
But Deuteronomy 25:5–10 addressed a particular situation: a man had died without leaving offspring, and his surviving brother was called to preserve the deceased brother’s family line.
The brother was not being given permission to pursue another man's wife while that man was alive.
The deceased brother's widow was not being treated as an object of desire.
The law addressed a vulnerable household facing the loss of its future.
This practice is commonly called levirate marriage, from the Latin word levir, meaning “husband’s brother.”
The Hebrew expression is even more revealing.
יָבָם — yavam
It means a husband’s brother in the context of this family obligation.
And the related Hebrew verb:
יָבַם — yavam
Refers to performing the duty of a husband’s brother.
This was not a loophole for lust.
It was a legal provision concerning family continuity, inheritance, and the welfare of a widow.
And if you want to understand why that mattered, you have to imagine the world in which these commandments were given.
Imagine a woman standing outside her home.
Her husband has died.
There is no son to carry his name.
No child to continue his household.
The future she imagined has collapsed.
In ancient Israel, family land, inheritance, and household identity were closely connected. A widow without children could face serious economic and social vulnerability.
The law did not erase her grief.
It did not guarantee that every family would treat her kindly.
But it established a particular responsibility within the deceased husband’s family.
Deuteronomy 25:6 explains the purpose:
“And it shall be, that the firstborn which she beareth shall succeed in the name of his brother which is dead, that his name be not put out of Israel.” — KJV
That final phrase carries enormous weight.
“That his name be not put out of Israel.”
The Hebrew says:
וְלֹא־יִמָּחֶה שְׁמוֹ מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל
Velo-yimmakheh shemo mi-Yisraʾel.
Meaning, “So that his name will not be wiped out from Israel.”
The purpose was not to reward the surviving brother with another wife.
It was to preserve the deceased brother’s name and family continuity.
The firstborn son of such a union would be associated with the deceased brother’s name and inheritance within Israel’s family structure.
And here is something important that often gets lost in popular explanations.
The surviving brother could refuse.
Deuteronomy 25:7–10 describes what happened when he would not fulfill the responsibility.
The widow could bring the matter before the elders.
She could publicly declare that he refused to preserve his brother’s name.
And a ceremony involving the removal of his sandal and a public expression of disgrace would follow.
The law therefore imposed a serious social obligation, but it did not authorize the community to force a marriage through physical compulsion.
That distinction matters.
Scripture records the responsibility, the refusal, and the public consequences.
It does not tell us to romanticize every ancient family arrangement or pretend that women in that world never experienced injustice.
Instead, it invites us to read the law carefully, within the covenant and society in which it was given.
And the more carefully we read, the more something begins to emerge.
God's law was not merely concerned with prohibiting wrongdoing.
It also addressed responsibility toward people who could be left behind.
One command protected marriage from unlawful sexual relations.
The other provided a narrowly defined family duty when a marriage had ended through death without offspring.
The prohibition and the exception were not enemies. They served different purposes within the same covenant law.
But this is where the story becomes darker.
Because centuries of biblical history remind us that knowing a commandment and obeying it are two very different things.
Long before Moses delivered the law at Sinai, Genesis 38 records a disturbing episode involving Judah, his sons, and a woman named Tamar.
Tamar married Judah’s son Er.
Er died.
Judah then instructed his son Onan to fulfill the duty of a brother-in-law and raise up offspring for his deceased brother.
Genesis 38:8 says:
“And Judah said unto Onan, Go in unto thy brother's wife, and marry her, and raise up seed to thy brother.” — KJV
This was before the formal legislation of Deuteronomy, showing that the underlying family custom was already known.
But Onan refused to fulfill the purpose of the obligation.
He engaged in sexual relations with Tamar while deliberately preventing conception because he knew the offspring would not be reckoned as his own.
Genesis 38:9 explicitly identifies his motive.
He did not want to raise up offspring for his brother.
And Genesis 38:10 tells us that what he did displeased the Lord.
This passage is often reduced to an argument about a particular sexual act.
But the immediate narrative emphasizes Onan's deliberate refusal to fulfill his family obligation, his selfish motive, and his treatment of Tamar.
He wanted the benefit of the relationship without accepting the responsibility attached to it.
And Tamar was left waiting for a future that Judah failed to provide.
Think about that.
A woman had already buried one husband.
Then another man exploited the situation.
Then her father-in-law failed to fulfill what he had promised.
Her life became entangled in grief, injustice, desperation, and a scandal that would eventually expose Judah’s own wrongdoing.
Yet the story does not end with Tamar being erased.
Genesis 38:26 records Judah's confession:
“She hath been more righteous than I...” — KJV
That does not mean every action in the chapter is presented as a model for believers to imitate.
The narrative is morally complicated.
But Judah was forced to acknowledge his own failure toward Tamar.
And here is the detail that should make you stop reading for a moment.
Tamar later appears in the genealogy of Jesus Christ.
Matthew 1:3 names her.
A woman whose story involved death, injustice, family failure, and public scandal was not forgotten in the biblical account of the Messiah’s ancestry.
God did not call evil good.
He did not excuse human wrongdoing.
But human sin did not prevent Him from accomplishing His redemptive purposes.
The scandal was real. But it was not the end of the story.
And perhaps that is where this ancient passage begins to reach into our own lives.
Because not everyone reading this has experienced a scandal that became public.
Some scandals remain hidden.
A betrayal nobody knows about.
A promise broken behind closed doors.
A family responsibility someone abandoned.
A marriage wounded by selfishness.
A person left carrying consequences they never chose.
Some people know what it feels like to be Tamar—not because their circumstances are identical, but because someone who owed them honesty and responsibility chose self-interest instead.
Others may recognize something of Judah.
The painful realization that we have judged another person while refusing to confront our own wrongdoing.
And still others may recognize Onan's selfishness.
Wanting the privileges of commitment without the sacrifices.
Wanting to receive without giving.
Wanting to be seen as righteous without surrendering what is wrong.
That is why Scripture must do more than satisfy our curiosity.
It must examine our hearts.
Not so we can drown in shame.
But so we can stop hiding from the truth that leads us toward repentance.
And the story continues.
Because another widow would eventually enter the biblical narrative.
Her name was Ruth.
She was a Moabite woman who had lost her husband.
Her mother-in-law, Naomi, had also experienced devastating loss.
Two women were walking into an uncertain future.
Ruth could have returned to the life she knew.
Instead, she remained with Naomi.
And in Ruth 1:16, she declared:
“...thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God.” — KJV
This was not merely a sentimental declaration.
It was a costly commitment.
Ruth was entering a land where she would be a foreigner, without the security she might once have expected.
She went to work gleaning grain.
She gathered what harvesters left behind.
And through God's providence, she came to the field of Boaz.
Now here is where careful Bible reading becomes essential.
Boaz was a family redeemer, but the book of Ruth does not describe him as the deceased husband's brother.
His role was connected to Israel’s wider kinship and redemption customs, including the preservation of family property and the deceased man’s name.
Ruth 4 brings together concerns about redemption, inheritance, marriage, and family continuity.
The narrative is related in purpose to the levirate law, but it is not simply an identical application of Deuteronomy 25.
Boaz was not merely following a romantic impulse.
He acted publicly, before witnesses, and addressed the rights of a nearer redeemer.
He treated the matter as a responsibility that required integrity.
And Ruth, once a grieving widow gathering leftover grain, became part of an extraordinary family story.
Ruth 4:17 tells us that her son was named Obed.
Obed became the father of Jesse.
Jesse became the father of David.
And from David’s royal line, according to the New Testament, came Jesus Christ.
Matthew 1:5 names Ruth in the genealogy of Jesus.
Tamar is there.
Ruth is there.
Two women with very different stories.
Both connected to family continuity in circumstances marked by loss and vulnerability.
Both remembered in the ancestry of the Messiah.
And now we begin to see why these ancient passages matter beyond the legal question that first caught our attention.
The Bible does not present the Messiah's genealogy as a spotless collection of people who never suffered, sinned, failed, or faced complicated circumstances.
It records real human histories.
And God worked through those histories without approving the evil within them.
That is grace.
Not the denial of sin.
Not the rewriting of evil into goodness.
But God's power to bring about His holy purposes even in a world deeply wounded by human failure.
And this brings us to the deepest connection of all.
Jesus Christ is not a levirate husband in the legal sense of Deuteronomy 25.
We must not force that identification onto the text.
But the biblical themes of family preservation, costly responsibility, and redemption prepare us to appreciate something even greater about Him.
Boaz was willing to bear a cost to act as a redeemer within his family.
Jesus Christ accomplished a redemption infinitely greater.
He did not merely preserve an earthly family name.
He gave Himself to redeem sinners.
Peter writes:
The Greek word translated “redeemed” in verse 18 is:
ἐλυτρώθητε — elytrōthēte
From the verb lytroō, meaning to ransom or redeem.
Peter's point is unmistakable.
Our redemption was not purchased with ordinary wealth.
It came through the precious blood of Jesus Christ.
And this is where the entire discussion reaches its most important truth.
The ancient law addressed the preservation of a deceased man's family name.
The Gospel announces that sinners who were spiritually dead can receive eternal life through the risen Son of God.
The law revealed holiness, boundaries, responsibility, and justice.
But the law could not make sinful humanity righteous by human effort.
Jesus fulfilled the law and the prophets (Matthew 5:17).
He bore our sins in His body on the tree (1 Peter 2:24).
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose again on the third day, according to the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).
The deepest human problem is not simply that we have been misunderstood, abandoned, or wounded.
It is that every one of us needs reconciliation with a holy God.
We have sinned.
We have fallen short of His glory.
And no amount of religious performance can purchase forgiveness.
But Jesus Christ came to save sinners.
Not by pretending sin was harmless.
Not by lowering God's holiness.
But by giving Himself as the sufficient sacrifice for our sins.
That is why the Gospel is not merely a message about getting another chance.
It is the announcement that forgiveness and new life are offered through the crucified and risen Christ.
And the invitation is personal.
You may have been betrayed.
You may have betrayed someone.
You may have spent years carrying shame over something you cannot undo.
You may be reading this while struggling with a secret you are terrified someone will discover.
But listen carefully.
Your past is not stronger than the saving power of Jesus Christ.
That does not mean every consequence disappears.
It does not mean repentance is unnecessary.
It does not mean people you harmed must immediately trust you again.
Grace is not permission to continue in sin.
Grace calls us to turn from sin and trust the Savior.
And when Christ saves a person, He does not merely give them a more respectable religious image.
He begins a work of transformation.
Second Corinthians 5:17 declares:
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.” — KJV
Do you see the beauty of that?
The Gospel does not say your sin was imaginary.
It says Christ is sufficient to save sinners.
The Gospel does not say your wounds never happened.
It says your suffering need not have the final word over your identity and hope.
The Gospel does not say every broken relationship will be restored exactly as it was.
It says reconciliation with God is possible through Jesus Christ.
And perhaps someone reading this needs to hear that more than anything else today.
You have spent so long defining yourself by the worst thing that happened to you.
Or the worst thing you ever did.
You have rehearsed your failures until they sound louder than God's promises.
You have wondered whether someone with your history could ever become useful in His kingdom.
Remember Tamar.
Remember Ruth.
Remember that the genealogy of Jesus contains people whose lives were touched by grief, injustice, scandal, and astonishing grace.
And then remember something greater.
Your hope is not that your story resembles theirs. Your hope is that Jesus Christ truly saves.
The God who revealed His holiness in Leviticus is not different from the God who revealed His mercy in Christ.
His holiness never stopped mattering.
His justice never disappeared.
His mercy was never an afterthought.
At the cross, we see how seriously God takes sin—and how astonishingly He has acted to save sinners.
Romans 3:26 describes God as both just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus.
That is not contradiction.
That is the glory of the Gospel.
And now, after everything we have discovered, return to the original question.
Why did one law forbid a brother from having sexual relations with his brother's wife, while another instructed a brother to marry his deceased brother's childless widow?
Because Scripture was addressing two different circumstances.
One was a prohibition protecting the boundaries of marriage.
The other was a particular covenantal family obligation after death, intended to preserve a deceased brother's name and household.
The exception did not cancel the ordinary prohibition.
It was a specifically defined provision within ancient Israel's law.
And Christians should not confuse that ancient civil and family arrangement with a universal command requiring men today to marry their deceased brothers' widows.
The New Testament does not impose such an obligation on the church.
In fact, when the Sadducees questioned Jesus about a woman who had been married successively to seven brothers, they drew directly upon the levirate tradition (Matthew 22:23–33).
Jesus did not treat the law as a contradiction.
He used their question to correct their misunderstanding of the resurrection.
He declared that in the resurrection, people neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like angels in heaven in that respect.
His answer lifted the conversation beyond the preservation of earthly family lines to the reality of resurrection life.
And suddenly the ancient question that began with marriage, death, and the preservation of a name points us toward a far greater hope.
Death does not have the final victory over those who belong to Christ.
That is what makes this more than an interesting Bible study.
Because every earthly family eventually confronts death.
Every human name, no matter how celebrated, belongs to a fragile life.
Every inheritance can be lost.
Every generation passes.
But Jesus Christ rose from the grave.
And those who belong to Him have the promise of eternal life.
Not because they preserved their own reputation.
Not because they never made mistakes.
Not because their family history was impressive.
But because their Savior lives.
So perhaps the most important question today is no longer, “Why did God make an exception to this law?”
Perhaps it is this:
Have you personally trusted the Redeemer to whom the Scriptures ultimately lead us?
Not merely admired Him.
Not merely shared Bible verses about Him.
Not merely defended Christianity in arguments.
Have you repented of your sin and placed your faith in Jesus Christ?
Because there is a difference between knowing the language of redemption and actually trusting the Redeemer.
You can understand the Hebrew.
You can memorize the Greek.
You can explain the legal distinction between Leviticus and Deuteronomy.
And still miss the Savior.
Please do not let that happen.
If something in this article has exposed an area of compromise, come honestly before God.
If you have abandoned a responsibility, seek to make things right.
If you have used someone else's vulnerability for selfish gain, repent.
If you have been wounded by another person's sin, bring that pain to Christ and seek wise, trustworthy support.
If you have been hiding behind religious appearances, stop pretending that appearances can heal your soul.
And if you have never trusted Jesus Christ, turn to Him today.
You do not need a polished testimony to come to the Savior.
You need the mercy that only He can give.
You can pray honestly:

“Lord Jesus, I confess that I have sinned and need Your forgiveness. I cannot save myself. I believe You died for sinners and rose again. I turn from my sin and place my trust in You. Teach me to follow You in truth, obedience, and love. Change what I cannot change by my own strength. Make my life a testimony to Your grace. Amen.”
The power is not in repeating particular words.
The hope is in Jesus Christ, who saves those who turn to Him in faith.
And if you are still reading, I want to ask you something personal.
What part of this story reached you?
Was it the holiness of God's boundaries?
The responsibility we owe one another?
The widow who feared being forgotten?
The man who chose selfishness?
The woman whose painful story was not erased?
Or the astonishing truth that Christ can redeem people whose lives are far from perfect?
And if you are struggling, you can simply comment, “Pray for me.”
You do not need to reveal private details or publicly confess something that should be addressed with a trusted pastor, counselor, or appropriate person.
Sometimes a simple request for prayer is enough to remind us that we were never meant to walk the Christian life alone.
Not because every difficult biblical question can be answered in a few sentences.
But because careful study matters.
Context matters.
Truth matters.
And when we read Scripture faithfully, we learn to distinguish what God actually said from what we merely assumed He meant.
A thoughtful share may reach someone who has been told that the Bible contradicts itself.
It may reach a believer struggling with difficult Old Testament laws.
It may reach a person who has quietly concluded that their past has placed them beyond God's mercy.
Not to pressure them.
But to invite them into a conversation worth having.
And if Gospel Warrior has been helping you grow in biblical understanding, I want to extend a deeper invitation.
Invite your family, your friends, fellow believers, those who have grown spiritually cold, and even those who are still searching for answers.
We want it to be a place where people return to Scripture, encounter the truth of the Gospel, ask honest questions, and grow in faithful obedience to Christ.
These resources are part of our desire to help believers grow deeper in the Word of God.
The Bible teaches us to support faithful ministry and give generously, but it also teaches that giving should be voluntary, not forced.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” — KJV
And it is certainly not a payment for God's favor.
These are simply tangible ways of thanking those who choose to stand with the ministry.
It is the opportunity to participate in making Christ-centered teaching and discipleship resources available to others.
Continue testing every teaching against Scripture.
Continue praying.
Continue gathering with faithful believers.
Continue growing in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ.
Because the goal of Gospel Warrior is not merely to build an audience.
It is to point people toward the One who alone can save.
And that brings us back to the widow, the brother, and the law that seemed impossible to reconcile.
What began as a difficult question about forbidden relationships became a window into holiness, covenant responsibility, human failure, and redemption.
We saw a law that established boundaries.
An exception designed for a specific family need.
A man who abused his responsibility.
A woman who suffered injustice.
A foreign widow who found refuge.
A family line that led to a king.
And a genealogy that eventually brought us to the birth of Jesus Christ.
But the most beautiful truth was never simply that certain names survived in ancient Israel.
It was that God was moving history toward the coming of His Son.
The Savior who entered a world full of broken families, wounded people, complicated histories, and sinners in desperate need of mercy.
He came without sin.
He died for sinners.
He rose victorious over death.
And He calls us to repentance and faith.
So when you close this article, do not remember only the exception to an ancient law.
Remember the Redeemer.
Remember that God's holiness is real.
Remember that His mercy is not cheap.
Remember that sin must be confronted, not concealed.
And remember that no human scandal is greater than the saving power of Jesus Christ.
The names people tried to erase may be forgotten by the world—but the soul Christ redeems is never forgotten by God.
